generative-ai-intro.title: Imagine designing a poster for a college festival
intro: Your team needs several poster ideas, a short invitation, and an announcement for the college website. A search engine can find existing posters; a classifier can identify whether a poster contains a face. A generative model can propose a new layout or draft new wording. This is useful when several answers could be acceptable, rather than when there is exactly one stored fact to retrieve.

The word “new” means a newly produced output, not a guarantee of originality or accuracy. A model can reproduce familiar phrases and sometimes training examples. You supply a task and constraints, inspect its candidates, and decide which parts are usable. The application is a drafting partner; you still own the final communication.
generative-ai-intro.mechanismTitle: How examples become a reusable model
mechanism: During training, the system adjusts internal numbers called parameters so that its outputs better match patterns in examples. Later, it reuses those numbers to generate. A prompt such as “write a cheerful invitation” guides this use-time process; it normally does not change the saved parameters.

We can see the idea without a large model. Train a tiny word-transition model on three invented invitations. It counts which word follows each word, then uses those counts to build a sentence. This is a genuine, very limited statistical text generator—not an LLM. Its limitations make the difference between learning a pattern and understanding a situation easy to inspect.
generative-ai-intro.labTitle: Python: learn word transitions and generate an invitation
generative-ai-intro.setup: Python 3, standard library only. No account, model download, or GPU. The three short training sentences below are invented. This example chooses the most frequent next word; ties follow their first occurrence.
generative-ai-intro.code:
from collections import Counter, defaultdict

sentences = [
    "join our science fair today",
    "join our science club today",
    "visit our science fair today",
]
counts = defaultdict(Counter)
for sentence in sentences:
    words = ["<start>"] + sentence.split() + ["<end>"]
    for current, following in zip(words, words[1:]):
        counts[current][following] += 1

word, result = "<start>", []
for _ in range(12):  # Bound generation even if a cycle appears.
    word = counts[word].most_common(1)[0][0]
    if word == "<end>":
        break
    result.append(word)

print("After science:", dict(counts["science"]))
print("Draft:", " ".join(result))
print("Different from every training sentence:",
      " ".join(result) not in sentences)
notes: Counter records observed transitions: after “science”, “fair” occurs twice and “club” once. Those are learned counts, not hand-written grammar rules.
The generation loop repeatedly selects, appends, and reuses a word. The stop marker and 12-step cap prevent an endless reply.
The final Boolean checks exact novelty against this tiny dataset. It cannot establish originality against the wider world.
generative-ai-intro.meaning: The most frequent path reproduces one of the training sentences. That is an important result: a generative process does not automatically create novel content. Larger models learn richer dependencies, but still need checks for copying, factual errors, and suitability.
generative-ai-intro.mistake: Do not confuse randomness with intelligence. Randomly picking words can produce variety without producing meaning; a useful model must learn relationships that make its combinations coherent.
generative-ai-intro.tryIt: Add two invitations containing “science exhibition”, then rerun. Which continuation after “science” wins?
generative-ai-intro.answer: Fair and exhibition now tie at two. With this deterministic first-occurrence tie rule, fair remains selected. Adding a third exhibition example makes exhibition the most frequent continuation.

generative-vs-discriminative.title: Recognizing a fruit is not the same task as drawing one
intro: Imagine a fruit shop with photographs of apples and oranges. A recognition system receives one photograph and returns a label. It needs features that separate the two fruits. A drawing system must also model how their shapes, colours, textures, and backgrounds fit together so that a new picture looks plausible.

Call the observed information x and the target label y. The notation p(y | x) means “the probability of a label after seeing the input”. A generative model may model p(x), or p(x, y) when labels are included. Here p means probability; the comma means considering the input and label together. Not every generator calculates an explicit probability, but it still learns a process that produces samples.
generative-vs-discriminative.mechanismTitle: Follow both routes to the same spam decision
mechanism: The distinction concerns what a model learns, not simply what its user sees. A classifier can learn the spam decision directly. A generative classifier can learn how spam and non-spam messages tend to be formed, then derive the decision. Both can finish by predicting “spam”.

In the email dataset above, there are 40 spam messages and 60 legitimate messages. Thirty spam messages contain “offer”; six legitimate messages contain it. The generative route combines each class frequency with its within-class “offer” frequency. Normalizing those two joint quantities produces the same conditional probability as directly counting 30 spam messages among 36 offer messages.
generative-vs-discriminative.labTitle: Python: two routes to an 83.3% spam estimate
generative-vs-discriminative.setup: Python 3, standard library only. These are counts from a constructed dataset, not measured spam-filter performance.
generative-vs-discriminative.code:
spam, legitimate = 40, 60
offer_spam, offer_legitimate = 30, 6
total = spam + legitimate

prior_spam = spam / total
prior_legitimate = legitimate / total
p_offer_given_spam = offer_spam / spam
p_offer_given_legitimate = offer_legitimate / legitimate

joint_spam = prior_spam * p_offer_given_spam
joint_legitimate = prior_legitimate * p_offer_given_legitimate
derived = joint_spam / (joint_spam + joint_legitimate)
direct = offer_spam / (offer_spam + offer_legitimate)

print(f"P(spam and offer): {joint_spam:.2f}")
print(f"P(legitimate and offer): {joint_legitimate:.2f}")
print(f"Generative route: {derived:.1%}")
print(f"Direct count: {direct:.1%}")
assert abs(derived - direct) < 1e-12
notes: A prior is the class probability before inspecting “offer”: 40/100 or 60/100.
Multiplication gives joint probabilities 0.30 and 0.06. Their sum, 0.36, is the probability of observing “offer”.
Dividing 0.30 by 0.36 restricts the answer to offer messages. This demonstrates probability arithmetic; it does not train a modern discriminative network.
generative-vs-discriminative.meaning: The final prediction alone cannot identify a model family. Ask whether training learned a direct decision rule or a model of the data-producing process. With more features, modelling choices and assumptions determine how well either approach generalizes.
generative-vs-discriminative.mistake: Do not assume that every text generator is a classifier or that generative classifiers always beat discriminative ones. The appropriate approach depends on the data, assumptions, and task.
generative-vs-discriminative.tryIt: If six more legitimate offer emails arrive, with no other changes, what happens to the direct estimate?
generative-vs-discriminative.answer: There are now 42 offer emails and still 30 spam offer emails: 30/42 ≈ 71.4%. Evidence that “offer” also occurs legitimately reduces its usefulness as a spam signal.
generative-vs-discriminative.output:
P(spam and offer): 0.30
P(legitimate and offer): 0.06
Generative route: 83.3%
Direct count: 83.3%

how-generative-models-learn.title: A bag of scene cards makes “distribution” concrete
intro: Imagine ten scene cards: five forests, three coasts, and two cities. Draw a card without looking, then return it. Forests should appear often, but not every draw. This pattern of relative frequencies is a distribution. Learning a distribution means estimating a pattern like this from examples rather than choosing every output in advance.

Real data has many interacting properties. A beach image includes water colour, horizon position, lighting, and objects. A model learns relationships among these properties, not merely a list of scene names. A latent representation is an internal numerical description that can capture some of those relationships; its individual coordinates need not correspond neatly to human concepts.
how-generative-models-learn.mechanismTitle: Separate the learned probabilities from the random draw
mechanism: A probability distribution says what can happen and how likely each outcome is. Sampling turns that description into one outcome. Divide the interval from zero to one into pieces with widths equal to the probabilities. A uniformly drawn number chooses whichever piece it falls in.

Conditioning means supplying extra information before that choice. “At sunset” changes which scenes or colours should be likely. It is like selecting from a different bag, using the same model. The comparison below keeps the random draw fixed so you can attribute the changed result to the condition rather than to a different random start.
how-generative-models-learn.labTitle: Python: fit frequencies, then sample with and without guidance
how-generative-models-learn.setup: Python 3, standard library only. Training here is counting scene labels. The sunset probabilities are invented separately so the conditioning effect is visible.
notes: Counter turns the training examples into frequencies; dividing by ten makes probabilities.
The cumulative total builds the intervals shown in the lesson. The comparison uses draw < cumulative, matching intervals that exclude their upper endpoint.
Fixed draws make the result reproducible. Replacing each draw with random.random() creates random samples instead.
how-generative-models-learn.meaning: At r=0.35, the ordinary distribution selects forest and the sunset distribution selects coast. No parameters were optimized during this comparison: only the supplied distribution changed. A neural conditional generator learns this relationship from paired examples instead of receiving a hand-written sunset table.
how-generative-models-learn.mistake: Matching label frequencies alone is not enough to generate convincing images. A generator must also learn within-class variation and relationships, and it may fail on conditions absent from training.
how-generative-models-learn.tryIt: Which category is selected at exactly r=0.50 in the ordinary distribution?
how-generative-models-learn.answer: Coast. Forest occupies [0, 0.50), so the boundary belongs to the next interval. Explicit boundary conventions prevent off-by-one-style sampling bugs.
how-generative-models-learn.output:
Learned: {'forest': 0.5, 'coast': 0.3, 'city': 0.2}
r=0.35: plain=forest, sunset=coast
r=0.72: plain=coast, sunset=coast
r=0.95: plain=city, sunset=city

vae.title: Compress a sketch, but leave room for variation
intro: Suppose you want to create new handwritten digits. An ordinary autoencoder learns to compress a digit into a few numbers and reconstruct it. But choosing arbitrary numbers between its compressed examples may lead to poor outputs: nothing necessarily taught the decoder how to use those gaps.

A VAE makes the compressed description probabilistic. For each input, its encoder predicts a centre and a spread. Sampling near that centre produces slightly different descriptions of the same input. A regularization objective encourages these distributions to resemble a simple reference distribution, making sampling more practical. This encourages useful organization; it does not guarantee every point decodes well.
vae.mechanismTitle: Read the centre, spread, sample, and reconstruction separately
mechanism: The mean μ specifies the centre. The standard deviation σ specifies the spread and must be positive. Epsilon ε is a random draw with mean zero and standard deviation one. Multiplying σ by ε scales that randomness; adding μ moves it to the correct centre. The symbol ⊙ means multiply corresponding coordinates.

Reconstruction loss measures how different the decoded output is from the input. KL divergence measures how different the encoded distribution is from the reference prior. In the common Gaussian case, each coordinate contributes ½(μ² + σ² − 1 − log(σ²)). Summing the coordinates gives the KL term. The prior is usually chosen as a standard normal; it is not automatically learned in this basic VAE.
vae.labTitle: Python: reproduce a latent sample and its KL penalty
vae.setup: Python 3, standard library only. This runs the VAE arithmetic on supplied encoder outputs; it is not a trained image generator.
vae.code:
import math

mu = [0.5, -1.0]
sigma = [0.5, 2.0]
epsilon = [0.4, -0.3]  # Chosen draws for a traceable example.
z = [m + s * e for m, s, e in zip(mu, sigma, epsilon)]
kl = sum(0.5 * (m*m + s*s - 1 - math.log(s*s))
         for m, s in zip(mu, sigma))

original = [0.0, 1.0, 1.0, 0.0]
reconstructed = [0.1, 0.8, 0.9, 0.2]  # Illustrative decoder output.
mse = sum((a-b)**2 for a, b in zip(original, reconstructed)) / 4
print("Sample z:", [round(v, 2) for v in z])
print(f"KL penalty: {kl:.3f}")
print(f"Reconstruction MSE: {mse:.3f}")
for beta in [0.1, 1.0]:
    print(f"beta={beta:.1f}: total={mse + beta*kl:.3f}")
notes: zip pairs matching coordinates, so the first sample is 0.5 + 0.5×0.4 = 0.7.
The KL expression compares two diagonal Gaussian distributions, with the reference fixed to mean zero and variance one.
The four squared pixel errors total 0.10; their mean is 0.025. The developer-chosen beta changes the balance, not the reconstruction itself in this calculation.
vae.meaning: A larger beta raises the penalty for a latent distribution far from the prior. In actual training, that changes the updates and can trade fine reconstruction detail for stronger latent regularity. Loss magnitudes also depend on whether pixel and latent terms are summed or averaged.
vae.mistake: Do not decode arbitrary latent values and assume realism. Check reconstructions and fresh prior samples separately. A near-zero KL with little response to z can indicate posterior collapse, but a single loss value is not a diagnosis.
vae.tryIt: What happens to the KL term if every mean becomes 0 and every standard deviation becomes 1?
vae.answer: Each coordinate contributes ½(0 + 1 − 1 − log(1)) = 0. The encoded Gaussian then matches the chosen standard-normal prior.
vae.output:
Sample z: [0.7, -1.6]
KL penalty: 1.750
Reconstruction MSE: 0.025
beta=0.1: total=0.200
beta=1.0: total=1.775

gans.title: A learner creates examples; another learner critiques them
intro: Imagine a student practising sketches while a teacher compares them with a collection of real examples. The student receives feedback on the sketches and tries again. A GAN uses two neural networks for a similar feedback loop: a generator creates samples, and a discriminator learns to distinguish generated samples from real ones.

The analogy has a limit: the discriminator is not a human judge of beauty or truth. It learns whatever clues distinguish the training examples from current generated examples. If the dataset contains shortcuts, such as a watermark, both networks can focus on the wrong thing. The quality of the data and the learning process matters.
gans.mechanismTitle: Why two losses point in different directions
mechanism: Let D(x) be the discriminator’s estimated probability that sample x is real. For a real sample we want D(x) near one; for a generated sample we want it near zero. The discriminator loss penalizes both kinds of mistake. During the generator update, a common non-saturating loss is −log(D(G(z))): the generator wants its sample to receive a higher “real” score.

The code below trains the smallest possible adversarial system. Real data consists of the number 2. The generator learns a number g; the discriminator is a sigmoid of w×x+b. Analytic derivatives replace a deep-learning library, so you can see which parameters change. This degenerate one-point distribution demonstrates alternating updates, not realistic image synthesis or diversity.
gans.labTitle: Python: run a tiny adversarial training loop
gans.setup: Python 3, standard library only. CPU training, no downloads. This scalar GAN is deliberately restricted to learning one target value.
gans.code:
import math

def sigmoid(x):
    return 1 / (1 + math.exp(-x))

g, w, b = -1.0, 0.5, 0.0
rate = 0.05
for step in range(1001):
    real_score = sigmoid(w * 2.0 + b)
    fake_score = sigmoid(w * g + b)
    if step in [0, 100, 500, 1000]:
        print(f"step={step:4d} generated={g:.3f} "
              f"D(real)={real_score:.3f} D(fake)={fake_score:.3f}")
    if step == 1000:
        break
    # Discriminator update: g is held fixed.
    dw = (real_score - 1) * 2.0 + fake_score * g
    db = (real_score - 1) + fake_score
    w -= rate * dw
    b -= rate * db
    # Generator update: use updated D, but do not update w or b.
    fake_score = sigmoid(w * g + b)
    dg = (fake_score - 1) * w
    g -= rate * dg
notes: sigmoid converts the discriminator’s raw numerical score into a value between zero and one.
The first update reduces discriminator error using a real target of one and a fake target of zero. The generator g stays fixed during this phase.
The second derivative follows the discriminator back to g. Only g is changed, while w and b are used as fixed feedback.
gans.meaning: Watch the generated value move toward the real value while the two scores change. The trajectory need not improve monotonically: each learner changes the problem faced by the other. A discriminator near 0.5 can also be undertrained, so inspect samples and diversity rather than declaring success from its score alone.
gans.mistake: A generator can learn a few outputs that fool the discriminator and neglect other real patterns. This is mode collapse. Compare many random inputs, class coverage, and held-out sample quality; a good-looking single image is weak evidence.
gans.tryIt: Why is this example unable to demonstrate mode collapse across several classes?
gans.answer: Its real distribution contains only one value and its generator has no random input. There are no distinct real modes to cover. A realistic diversity test needs varied data and multiple latent inputs.
gans.output:
step=   0 generated=-1.000 D(real)=0.731 D(fake)=0.378
step= 100 generated=1.851 D(real)=0.574 D(fake)=0.543
step= 500 generated=1.463 D(real)=0.542 D(fake)=0.569
step=1000 generated=1.963 D(real)=0.501 D(fake)=0.502

diffusion-models.title: Learn to remove corruption before trying to invent an image
intro: Think of a clean drawing gradually covered with speckles. Early on you can still see the outline; later it becomes almost impossible. Diffusion training creates many such corrupted examples and teaches a model how to estimate the corruption. The difficulty is controlled, so the model learns at several noise levels rather than only one.

Generation reverses the idea: begin with noise and use many model-guided updates to form structure. The network does not simply reveal a hidden original image underneath the starting noise. Its learned patterns and any supplied condition influence which of many plausible outputs emerges.
diffusion-models.mechanismTitle: Trace one noisy value before scaling up to an image
mechanism: A timestep t identifies a noise level. The schedule determines how much clean signal and noise to mix at that level. The cumulative signal factor ᾱₜ lies between zero and one; its square root scales the clean value. The square root of 1−ᾱₜ scales the sampled noise.

After seeing the noisy value and the timestep, a noise-prediction model estimates ε. An estimate of the clean value is x̂₀ = (xₜ − √(1−ᾱₜ) ε̂) / √ᾱₜ. This rearranges the forward-noising equation; it is not the complete multi-step reverse sampler. A scheduler still decides the next noise level and any additional randomness.
diffusion-models.labTitle: Python: see how noise-prediction error affects reconstruction
diffusion-models.setup: Python 3, standard library only. A one-value calculation with known noise, not a trained denoising network. The estimates below are chosen to isolate their effect.
diffusion-models.code:
import math

clean = 0.80
alpha_bar = 0.64
noise = -0.50
signal_scale = math.sqrt(alpha_bar)
noise_scale = math.sqrt(1 - alpha_bar)
noisy = signal_scale * clean + noise_scale * noise
print(f"Noisy value: {noisy:.3f}")

for estimated_noise in [-0.50, -0.40, -0.20]:
    estimated_clean = (noisy - noise_scale * estimated_noise) / signal_scale
    noise_mse = (noise - estimated_noise) ** 2
    print(f"noise estimate={estimated_noise:.2f}, "
          f"clean estimate={estimated_clean:.3f}, "
          f"noise MSE={noise_mse:.3f}")
notes: With perfect noise prediction, subtracting the known noise contribution and undoing the signal scaling recovers 0.80.
The loop varies only the estimate. The increasing discrepancy makes the training objective’s purpose visible.
diffusion-models.meaning: Better noise estimates recover a cleaner signal in this controlled calculation. At extremely low signal levels, small estimation errors can be amplified. Real diffusion models therefore use timestep-aware training and carefully designed reverse updates rather than repeatedly applying this equation blindly.
diffusion-models.mistake: A noise-prediction target, a clean-sample target, and a velocity target are different parameterizations. The training objective and scheduler must agree; using a formula from a different parameterization can break sampling.
diffusion-models.tryIt: Keep the noisy value fixed but set the estimated noise to zero. What clean estimate do you get?
diffusion-models.answer: 0.34/0.8 = 0.425. Treating the corruption as absent leaves a substantial error compared with the original 0.80.
diffusion-models.output:
Noisy value: 0.340
noise estimate=-0.50, clean estimate=0.800, noise MSE=0.000
noise estimate=-0.40, clean estimate=0.725, noise MSE=0.010
noise estimate=-0.20, clean estimate=0.575, noise MSE=0.090

stable-latent-diffusion.title: Why a smaller workspace makes repeated image generation practical
intro: Imagine planning a mural with a small sketch before painting the full wall. A compact workspace can make repeated revisions cheaper. Latent diffusion uses an analogous idea: it performs the expensive repeated denoising in a compressed numerical representation, then turns the result into pixels.

The compression is learned, not an ordinary resized thumbnail. A VAE encoder maps images into latent values, and its decoder reconstructs images from those values. A latent channel is a learned feature map, not necessarily red, green, or blue. The sketch analogy explains the size advantage but should not be mistaken for the actual encoding operation.
stable-latent-diffusion.mechanismTitle: Follow the prompt branch and the image branch together
mechanism: In a common Stable Diffusion-style pipeline, the prompt is split into text pieces and a text encoder turns them into numerical representations. These guide a denoising network operating on the noisy latent. Cross-attention is a mechanism that lets latent locations use relevant text representations; it is not a separate image painted by the text encoder.

The scheduler uses the denoiser prediction to update the latent, repeating for the chosen number of steps. The VAE decoder runs on the final latent to produce the image. Pure text-to-image generation starts from random latent noise; image-to-image also uses the encoder to obtain a starting latent from the supplied image. Architectures vary: a Transformer may replace a U-Net denoiser, and the example dimensions are not universal.
stable-latent-diffusion.labTitle: Python: calculate representation size and memory
stable-latent-diffusion.setup: Python 3, standard library only. This is a tensor-size calculator, not a Stable Diffusion implementation. It estimates the storage for one tensor, excluding model weights, activations, workspace, and allocator overhead.
stable-latent-diffusion.code:
from math import prod

pixels = (1, 3, 512, 512)  # batch, channels, height, width
latent = (1, 4, 64, 64)
bytes_per_value = 2  # Developer assumption: float16.

for name, shape in [("pixels", pixels), ("latent", latent)]:
    values = prod(shape)
    mib = values * bytes_per_value / (1024 ** 2)
    print(f"{name}: shape={shape}, values={values:,}, MiB={mib:.5f}")

print(f"Spatial-location ratio: {(512*512)/(64*64):.0f}x")
print(f"Scalar-value ratio: {prod(pixels)/prod(latent):.0f}x")
notes: prod multiplies all dimensions. Batch size one means the count describes one image.
Spatial locations shrink by 8×8=64. Four latent channels versus three image channels changes the scalar-value ratio to 48.
Multiplying by two gives the assumed byte count; dividing by 1024² converts bytes to MiB.
stable-latent-diffusion.meaning: The latent tensor is much smaller, which explains why repeated work there can be efficient. A 48× reduction in scalar count does not imply exactly 48× less latency or total GPU memory: layer structure, attention, precision, and other tensors also matter.
stable-latent-diffusion.mistake: Do not use a latent from one checkpoint with an unrelated decoder or ignore the pipeline’s latent scaling. Compatible tensor dimensions alone do not guarantee compatible learned representations.
stable-latent-diffusion.tryIt: If image width and height both double, while the compression factor stays eight, how does the number of latent values change?
stable-latent-diffusion.answer: It becomes four times larger: 4×128×128 rather than 4×64×64. Doubling both spatial dimensions multiplies area by four.
stable-latent-diffusion.output:
pixels: shape=(1, 3, 512, 512), values=786,432, MiB=1.50000
latent: shape=(1, 4, 64, 64), values=16,384, MiB=0.03125
Spatial-location ratio: 64x
Scalar-value ratio: 48x

controlling-diffusion-models.title: Ask for a change without losing what matters
intro: You have a product photo and want a different background, but the product must keep its shape. A longer text prompt alone may not reliably protect it. First decide what should stay fixed and what may change. A mask can specify a region; a pose or edge map can specify geometry; a reference image can provide a starting appearance.

These controls answer different questions. The random seed chooses a starting random state. A prompt describes desired content. Guidance changes how strongly conditioning influences a denoising prediction. None of these is an absolute guarantee: inspect the resulting image against the actual constraint, especially at mask boundaries and fine details.
controlling-diffusion-models.mechanismTitle: A mask controls location; guidance controls a direction
mechanism: Picture a mask as a grid aligned with the source image. In this lesson’s convention, one means “replace this position” and zero means “keep it”. Each output position chooses between the original and a candidate. A real inpainting pipeline denoises using surrounding context; our small example isolates only the final mask logic.

Classifier-free guidance compares an unconditional noise prediction with a conditional one. Their difference is a direction toward the supplied condition, and the scale multiplies that difference. At scale zero the unconditional prediction remains; at scale one the conditional prediction remains. Larger values extrapolate beyond it and may introduce saturation or artifacts.
controlling-diffusion-models.labTitle: Python: apply a mask and inspect guidance scales
controlling-diffusion-models.setup: Python 3, standard library only. These are toy grayscale values and scalar denoising predictions. This code composites given candidates; it does not synthesize an inpainted image.
controlling-diffusion-models.code:
source = [[1, 1, 1], [1, 9, 1], [1, 1, 1]]
candidate = [[4, 4, 4], [4, 2, 4], [4, 4, 4]]
mask = [[0, 0, 0], [0, 1, 0], [0, 0, 0]]
result = [
    [candidate[r][c] if mask[r][c] else source[r][c]
     for c in range(3)] for r in range(3)
]
print("Edited grid:")
for row in result:
    print(row)
unconditional, conditional = 0.2, 0.5
for scale in [0, 1, 3]:
    guided = unconditional + scale * (conditional - unconditional)
    print(f"scale={scale}: guided prediction={guided:.2f}")
notes: The nested loops visit every position and replace only the centre, where the mask contains one.
Changing the mask convention without changing the conditional expression would edit the wrong region.
The guidance values are predictions of noise-related quantities, not displayable pixel brightness or probabilities.
controlling-diffusion-models.meaning: The border remains unchanged while the centre changes from 9 to 2. Guidance independently produces 0.20, 0.50, and 1.10. Separating these operations helps diagnose whether a bad result came from the permitted region or from generation settings.
controlling-diffusion-models.mistake: Keep the seed, model version, scheduler, dimensions, and other settings fixed when comparing one control. Otherwise a different random start can masquerade as the effect of a changed prompt.
controlling-diffusion-models.tryIt: Set every mask value to one. What changes, and what does this say about the mask’s role?
controlling-diffusion-models.answer: The entire candidate grid is selected. The mask only decides where candidate content may replace the source; it cannot ensure the candidate itself is good.
controlling-diffusion-models.output:
Edited grid:
[1, 1, 1]
[1, 2, 1]
[1, 1, 1]
scale=0: guided prediction=0.20
scale=1: guided prediction=0.50
scale=3: guided prediction=1.10

finetuning-image-models.title: Teach a model a particular product, not just “a product”
intro: A prompt can ask for a blue mug, but your company may need the same distinctive mug in many scenes. Fine-tuning uses example images to adapt learned values so that the model better represents that subject or style. It differs from supplying a reference at generation time: a training process produces reusable changed parameters or an adapter.

Choose examples that separate the subject from accidental surroundings. Photograph the mug from different angles and against different backgrounds, with permission to use the images. If every example contains the same table, the model may learn “mug plus table” as one inseparable concept.
finetuning-image-models.mechanismTitle: Understand what a low-rank adapter adds
mechanism: A weight matrix maps one set of numbers into another. Full fine-tuning changes that matrix directly. LoRA keeps the base matrix W fixed and learns a smaller update BA, where A compresses the input to r coordinates and B expands it again. The rank r is a developer-chosen capacity setting.

For a 4×4 base and rank one, A has four numbers and B has four numbers. Their product is a 4×4 update, even though only eight values were learned. The effective operation is Wx + B(Ax), ignoring an optional scaling factor for clarity. The base still occupies memory; fewer trainable values is not the same as removing the original model.
finetuning-image-models.labTitle: Python: follow one input through the LoRA side path
finetuning-image-models.setup: Python 3, standard library only. Supplied adapter values illustrate matrix arithmetic after training; this is not an image fine-tuning run.
finetuning-image-models.code:
x = [1, 2, 0, -1]
A = [0.1, 0.2, 0.0, -0.1]  # A has shape [1, 4].
B = [1.0, 0.0, 0.5, -0.5]  # B has shape [4, 1].
base_output = x[:]  # Choose identity W for easy checking.
compressed = sum(a * v for a, v in zip(A, x))
update = [b * compressed for b in B]
adapted = [base + change for base, change in zip(base_output, update)]

print(f"A times x: {compressed:.2f}")
print("Adapter update:", [round(v, 2) for v in update])
print("Adapted output:", [round(v, 2) for v in adapted])
print("Base parameters:", 4 * 4)
print("Trainable adapter parameters:", len(A) + len(B))
notes: B scales that one intermediate value into four update values. Adding the update to the base output preserves the original computation plus a learned adjustment.
The identity base is chosen only to make every operation traceable. Real projection matrices contain learned values.
finetuning-image-models.meaning: The adapter changes the output without replacing the base matrix. In actual training, only selected adapter values receive updates. A rank that is too small may lack capacity; larger ranks increase training cost and can overfit a small dataset.
finetuning-image-models.mistake: Keep a final test set separate from both training and repeated validation-based decisions. Test the learned subject in new backgrounds and poses; training reconstruction alone cannot show generalization.
finetuning-image-models.tryIt: If r becomes two for the same 4×4 matrix, how many adapter values are learned?
finetuning-image-models.answer: A has 2×4=8 and B has 4×2=8, for 16 total. At this tiny size, rank two already matches the base parameter count; large real matrices are where low rank is more economical.
finetuning-image-models.output:
A times x: 0.60
Adapter update: [0.6, 0.0, 0.3, -0.3]
Adapted output: [1.6, 2.0, 0.3, -1.3]
Base parameters: 16
Trainable adapter parameters: 8

multimodal-ai.title: Read the picture and the question together
intro: A student uploads a photograph of a damaged bicycle and asks, “Which part needs attention?” The image carries evidence that the words alone do not contain. A useful system must connect that evidence with the question before generating an answer; simply producing fluent bicycle advice is not enough.

A modality is a kind of information, such as text, an image, or sound. Different encoders convert these inputs into numerical representations. Alignment makes related representations comparable; fusion combines information so that a later prediction can depend on more than one input. These are related ideas, not interchangeable operations.
multimodal-ai.mechanismTitle: Similarity is a clue, not proof of a specific claim
mechanism: Suppose a text encoder maps “a bicycle with a damaged wheel” to a vector—a short list of numbers. An image encoder maps each candidate image to a vector in a compatible space. Cosine similarity compares their directions, after accounting for their lengths. A larger value can help retrieve a related image.

The two-coordinate example below is deliberately invented. Real embeddings have many coordinates with learned meanings. Even a high similarity score cannot prove that a particular spoke is broken. For specific visual claims, inspect the relevant region and allow uncertainty when the resolution or visibility is insufficient.
multimodal-ai.labTitle: Python: compare an image representation with a text representation
multimodal-ai.setup: Python 3, standard library only. These vectors are illustrative and are not embeddings produced by a trained model.
notes: The dot product adds corresponding coordinate products. The denominator removes vector-length effects.
All vectors here already have length one, so A scores 0.8×0.6 + 0.6×0.8 = 0.96.
max selects a retrieval candidate. It does not generate a caption or verify every object in the image.
multimodal-ai.meaning: A is most aligned with the text in this toy space; B is orthogonal and C points in the opposite direction. To test a real multimodal system, keep the question fixed while replacing the image, then check whether its answer follows the changed evidence.
multimodal-ai.mistake: Never treat an OCR reading or broad image similarity as an authority to execute instructions found inside a picture. Source media is evidence to analyze, not trusted application instructions.
multimodal-ai.tryIt: Multiply every coordinate of image A by ten. Does its cosine similarity change?
multimodal-ai.answer: No. Its direction remains the same, and the numerator and vector norm grow by the same factor. This is why cosine similarity differs from an unnormalized dot product.
multimodal-ai.output:
Image A: 0.96
Image B: 0.00
Image C: -1.00
Top candidate: A

audio-music-video-generation.title: A good moment is not enough: sound and video must hold together
intro: Listen to an announcement that suddenly changes speaker halfway through, or watch a clip where a cup disappears between frames. Individual sounds or pictures may seem plausible, but the sequence fails. Temporal generation must preserve relationships across time as well as produce convincing local details.

Sound is recorded as a sequence of amplitude measurements. The sample rate tells us how many measurements occur per second. Video is a sequence of images; its frame rate tells us how many images occur per second. Audio samples and video frames are different units, and their rates must not be confused.
audio-music-video-generation.mechanismTitle: From a waveform to speech, music, and motion
mechanism: A waveform plots amplitude against time. A spectrogram instead shows how energy at different frequencies changes over time: one axis is time, another is frequency, and colour indicates strength. Speech systems may generate acoustic representations and use a vocoder—a model converting those representations into sound—to produce the waveform.

Symbolic music can describe notes, start times, and durations before a synthesizer renders them as audio. Video generation may share information across frames so that objects and camera motion remain consistent. Text-to-video starts from a description, while image-to-video must also preserve relevant appearance from the starting image. Consent is essential when reproducing identifiable voices or likenesses.
audio-music-video-generation.labTitle: Python: generate a tiny waveform and measure frame consistency
audio-music-video-generation.setup: Python 3, standard library only. This creates a mathematical tone, not neural speech or music. The frame positions are invented to demonstrate a consistency check.
audio-music-video-generation.code:
import math

sample_rate = 8000
duration = 0.01
frequency = 1000
samples = [0.5 * math.sin(2 * math.pi * frequency * n / sample_rate)
           for n in range(round(sample_rate * duration))]
print("Audio samples:", len(samples))
print("First 8:", [round(v, 3) for v in samples[:8]])

smooth_positions = [0, 1, 2, 3, 4]
jump_positions = [0, 1, 7, 3, 4]
for name, positions in [("smooth", smooth_positions), ("jump", jump_positions)]:
    changes = [abs(b-a) for a, b in zip(positions, positions[1:])]
    print(f"{name}: frame displacements={changes}, maximum={max(changes)}")
notes: sample_rate×duration determines the number of audio samples: 8000×0.01 = 80.
The sine function generates a periodic tone. Frequency controls cycles per second, while the 0.5 multiplier controls peak amplitude.
Adjacent-frame differences detect the large jump, but the acceptable displacement depends on object speed and frame rate.
audio-music-video-generation.meaning: The waveform’s first eight values form one cycle because 8000/1000 = eight samples per cycle. The position check reveals a temporal jump that a single-frame beauty score would miss. Neither check measures naturalness, speech intelligibility, musical structure, or semantic correctness.
audio-music-video-generation.mistake: Upsampling a low-resolution recording does not recreate missing sound detail. Similarly, duplicating video frames increases the frame count without learning realistic intermediate motion.
audio-music-video-generation.tryIt: How many samples and video frames are needed for two seconds at 16 kHz audio and 24 frames per second?
audio-music-video-generation.answer: 32,000 mono audio samples and 48 video frames. Stereo audio needs two amplitude values per sampling instant, so its scalar-value count doubles.
audio-music-video-generation.output:
Audio samples: 80
First 8: [0.0, 0.354, 0.5, 0.354, 0.0, -0.354, -0.5, -0.354]
smooth: frame displacements=[1, 1, 1, 1], maximum=1
jump: frame displacements=[1, 6, 4, 1], maximum=6

synthetic-data.title: Create useful practice cases without pretending they are observations
intro: A delivery company wants to test its system on rainy-day delays, but its dataset contains few rainy days. A simulator or generative model could produce additional practice cases. The aim is not merely to fill a spreadsheet: the generated records must preserve useful relationships and make the downstream system work better on real deliveries.

Start by stating why each synthetic example is needed. Matching the population distribution and deliberately oversampling a rare case are different goals. A training dataset can intentionally emphasize rare events, while the real test set should still represent the environment in which performance will be judged.
synthetic-data.mechanismTitle: Preserve relationships, not just separate column averages
mechanism: Suppose larger orders normally cost more. Generating quantity and total price independently could create a ten-item order cheaper than a one-item order. In a rule-based simulator, encode the relationship explicitly. A learned generator would need to infer it from examples and would still require consistency checks.

The exercise below uses only invented product prices and random choices. It creates new records without consulting personal data, then verifies their business arithmetic. This is a useful software-testing dataset but not evidence that the records match real buying behaviour. For model-training utility, compare against real-data baselines on an untouched real test set.
synthetic-data.labTitle: Python: synthesize orders and validate the price relationship
synthetic-data.setup: Python 3, standard library only. All product names and prices are fictional. The seed makes this local simulation repeatable.
synthetic-data.code:
import random

rng = random.Random(7)
prices = {"notebook": 40, "pen": 10}
orders = []
for order_id in range(1, 6):
    product = rng.choice(list(prices))
    quantity = rng.randint(1, 3)
    orders.append({"id": order_id, "product": product,
                   "quantity": quantity, "total": prices[product] * quantity})

for order in orders:
    print(order)
valid = all(o["total"] == prices[o["product"]] * o["quantity"] for o in orders)
print("All totals valid:", valid)
print("Unique product/quantity combinations:",
      len({(o["product"], o["quantity"]) for o in orders}))
notes: The random generator varies product and quantity, while the multiplication preserves a known relationship.
Validation recomputes each total rather than trusting the generator.
The combination count measures limited coverage, not statistical fidelity or privacy. IDs are excluded because every generated ID is unique by construction.
synthetic-data.meaning: You obtain valid but narrow test records. Repeated combinations are possible, and important cases such as refunds, discounts, or unusual quantities are missing. Good synthetic-data design includes explicit coverage targets and tests beyond the happy path.
synthetic-data.mistake: Removing names from a training dataset is not a proof that a learned generator cannot leak information. Rare combinations, close copies, and membership signals can remain. Evaluate privacy separately from realism and utility.
synthetic-data.tryIt: Which test will fail if you increase one generated total by 1?
synthetic-data.answer: The recomputed-total check becomes false. A record can satisfy a JSON schema and still violate a business relationship, which is why both kinds of checks matter.

evaluating-generative-models.title: Evaluate the work the user needs, not the most impressive demo
intro: Two image generators produce attractive pictures. Which should a shop use for catalogue drafts? A single favourite image cannot answer that question. The shop also needs accurate product colour, varied backgrounds, consistent response time, and a tolerable cost for images that an editor actually accepts.

An evaluation set is a collection of representative requests held apart from tuning. A rubric states what counts as success on each request. For example, “the product colour matches the supplied reference” is more testable than “looks good”. Reviewers should assess candidates without model-name bias when possible, and disagreements should be examined rather than silently averaged away.
evaluating-generative-models.mechanismTitle: Build a report that can support a decision
mechanism: Measure quality, coverage, safety, latency, and cost separately. A hard gate is a requirement that must pass, such as no critical disclosures or a response-time limit. A preference score is useful only among candidates that satisfy those gates. Combining everything into a weighted average can hide an unacceptable failure behind several minor gains.

The p95 latency is a high-end response-time statistic. In the nearest-rank convention used below, sort N observations and take position ceil(0.95×N). With ten observations, that is the slowest value. Different percentile methods can interpolate, so state the convention; a tiny sample gives a very uncertain estimate of production behaviour.
evaluating-generative-models.labTitle: Python: compute acceptance, p95 latency, and cost per accepted output
evaluating-generative-models.setup: Python 3, standard library only. The observations are invented to teach measurement. Ten runs are not enough for a reliable release evaluation.
evaluating-generative-models.code:
import math

latencies = [1.0, 1.2, 1.4, 1.5, 1.7, 1.8, 2.0, 2.2, 2.8, 4.5]
accepted = [True, True, True, False, True, True, True, False, True, True]
cost_per_attempt = 0.03
p95 = sorted(latencies)[math.ceil(0.95 * len(latencies)) - 1]
acceptance = sum(accepted) / len(accepted)
cost_per_accepted = len(accepted) * cost_per_attempt / sum(accepted)
passes = acceptance >= 0.90 and p95 <= 3.0

print(f"Acceptance: {acceptance:.0%}")
print(f"Nearest-rank p95: {p95:.1f} s")
print(f"Cost per accepted output: {cost_per_accepted:.4f}")
print("Pass both gates:", passes)
notes: Boolean values contribute one for accepted and zero for rejected, giving eight accepted outputs out of ten.
The cost includes all attempts, including rejected ones: 10×0.03 divided by eight.
The final Boolean applies two independently chosen gates. Neither an average score nor a good-looking sample overrides a failed gate.
evaluating-generative-models.meaning: The system fails both the 90% acceptance requirement and the three-second p95 requirement. The cost of a useful output is higher than the cost of one attempt. Investigate which cases fail and whether the fix improves the same held-out workload, not a newly selected easier set.
evaluating-generative-models.mistake: FID compares image-set feature statistics, not the factual correctness of a caption or whether one specific image followed its prompt. Use task-appropriate instruments and report sample size, settings, and uncertainty.
evaluating-generative-models.tryIt: If the same total cost produces only five accepted outputs, what happens to cost per accepted output?
evaluating-generative-models.answer: It becomes 0.30/5 = 0.06, twice the cost per attempt. Rejection and retry rates directly affect practical economics.
evaluating-generative-models.output:
Acceptance: 80%
Nearest-rank p95: 4.5 s
Cost per accepted output: 0.0375
Pass both gates: False

responsible-generative-ai.title: Make a risk concrete enough to prevent and investigate
intro: A shop asks a model to draft product descriptions. One draft invents a safety certification; another includes a customer email copied from an inappropriate input. “Use AI carefully” does not tell the shop what to do. It needs named risks, approved sources, responsible reviewers, and a way to stop publication when checks fail.

Separate a possibility from a measured outcome. A likelihood-and-impact score is a planning tool selected by a team, not a scientific probability of harm. It helps prioritize work, but some severe failures warrant a hard stop regardless of their score. This lesson discusses engineering controls, not legal advice or a compliance guarantee.
responsible-generative-ai.mechanismTitle: Turn each risk into a control, owner, and test
mechanism: Prevention reduces the chance of a problem: approved input sources and access controls can keep sensitive records out of the request. Detection looks for a problem before or after generation: evidence checks and review can catch unsupported claims. Containment limits the consequence: drafts should not publish themselves. Recovery provides a correction and escalation path after a failure.

The toy review queue below uses explicit scenario metadata so that the control flow is easy to see. A real system must obtain these signals from trustworthy checks and reviewers; a model saying “safe=true” is not independent verification. Record only the minimum information needed for investigation, with access and retention controls.
responsible-generative-ai.labTitle: Python: route draft scenarios to an appropriate review path
responsible-generative-ai.setup: Python 3, standard library only. Rule-based routing over constructed cases; not a content-safety classifier and not proof that unflagged content is safe.
notes: The order gives a privacy concern priority even when other checks pass.
Missing evidence routes to clarification instead of encouraging the generator to guess.
Even the low-risk passing case goes to an editor. This is the intended-use policy for this example, not a universal requirement for every application.
responsible-generative-ai.meaning: The same model output can require different handling depending on its evidence, exposure, and consequences. Responsible operation is a workflow property as well as a model property. Every queue also needs a real owner and response process; a status label alone does not resolve an incident.
responsible-generative-ai.mistake: A keyword blocklist is not a complete safety mechanism. It can miss paraphrases and block harmless uses. Test false negatives, false positives, subgroup differences, and whether affected users can appeal or correct mistakes.
responsible-generative-ai.tryIt: Case A also lacks evidence. Which branch runs and why?
responsible-generative-ai.answer: The privacy block runs first. Multiple issues may still need recording and resolution, but the most urgent containment action must not be bypassed by a less severe check.
responsible-generative-ai.output:
A -> BLOCK and escalate privacy review
B -> REQUEST supporting evidence
C -> REQUIRE specialist approval
D -> SEND draft to editor

choosing-generative-model.title: Write the acceptance test before picking a model
intro: A design team wants to replace image backgrounds while keeping products unchanged. Start with that job, not a leaderboard. The candidate must support the required editing workflow, operate in an approved environment, fit the team’s latency limit, and produce acceptable results on their actual products.

A model family is only a starting shortlist. Two diffusion checkpoints can differ in their inputs, licences, memory requirements, and editing support. Likewise, an inexpensive hosted service may become costly if many attempts are rejected. The decision concerns the complete system under the intended workload.
choosing-generative-model.mechanismTitle: Use a shortlist, then an experiment
mechanism: First remove candidates that fail non-negotiable requirements. Then compare the remaining choices on the same prompts, cases, settings, and serving environment. Record versions and disclose differences you cannot control. Repeat important stochastic cases; otherwise one lucky sample can determine the winner.

For eligible choices, cost per accepted result is often more meaningful than cost per request. If a request costs 0.04 and 80% of attempts are accepted, the long-run cost per acceptance is approximately 0.04/0.80 = 0.05. This assumes comparable attempt costs and a representative acceptance rate, not a promise about any provider.
choosing-generative-model.labTitle: Python: filter candidates before comparing effective cost
choosing-generative-model.setup: Python 3, standard library only. Fictional candidates and measurements; these are not recommendations for commercial models.
choosing-generative-model.code:
models = [
    {"name": "A", "mask": False, "approved": True, "p95": 2.4, "cost": 0.01, "accept": 0.9},
    {"name": "B", "mask": True, "approved": True, "p95": 3.6, "cost": 0.04, "accept": 0.8},
    {"name": "C", "mask": True, "approved": True, "p95": 5.1, "cost": 0.02, "accept": 0.9},
    {"name": "D", "mask": True, "approved": True, "p95": 3.2, "cost": 0.03, "accept": 0.5},
]
eligible = [m for m in models
            if m["mask"] and m["approved"] and m["p95"] <= 4.0]
for model in eligible:
    effective = model["cost"] / model["accept"]
    print(f'{model["name"]}: cost per accepted={effective:.3f}')
winner = min(eligible, key=lambda m: m["cost"] / m["accept"])
print("Eligible:", [m["name"] for m in eligible])
print("Lowest effective cost:", winner["name"])
notes: The list comprehension applies all hard requirements before looking at price.
B costs more per attempt than D, but its higher acceptance rate lowers its effective cost.
min chooses among the already eligible models. A production selector must also handle an empty shortlist and uncertain acceptance estimates.
choosing-generative-model.meaning: B wins this particular cost comparison; that does not make it universally best. A team might choose another eligible model for quality, operations, or accessibility requirements not represented in the toy data. Make those criteria explicit before the experiment.
choosing-generative-model.mistake: Do not fine-tune solely because a larger model exists. First determine whether the failure is missing evidence, poor task instructions, an unsupported input, inadequate control, or genuinely missing learned capability.
choosing-generative-model.tryIt: If no candidate meets the latency gate, should you simply pick the fastest one and call it eligible?
choosing-generative-model.answer: No. Report that the shortlist is empty. Change the architecture, optimize, find another candidate, or explicitly renegotiate the product requirement before proceeding.
choosing-generative-model.output:
B: cost per accepted=0.050
D: cost per accepted=0.060
Eligible: ['B', 'D']
Lowest effective cost: B

building-genai-apps.title: A meeting-summary assistant must do more than write nice sentences
intro: After a project meeting, a team wants decisions and action items. A model can draft a summary, but the application must ensure it used the right transcript, did not invent an owner, returned the required fields, and did not create tasks before someone approved them.

Design the flow around an explicit contract. A schema describes the required structure, such as a list of decisions and a list of actions. An evidence rule describes what supports each value. A permission rule describes who may approve a consequential action. These contracts solve different problems and should be checked separately.
mechanism: Treat the model response as untrusted input. Parse it, validate field types, and then compare important claims against approved evidence. If required information is absent, return a useful clarification instead of filling the gap with a plausible guess. For arbitrary prose, evidence checking may require a reviewer or a more sophisticated retrieval-and-verification process.

The program below isolates this application boundary. Three fixed strings stand in for model responses so every branch can be reproduced offline. Its narrow semantic check matches an owner/task pair against a structured meeting record. This is real validation code, not a real model call and not a general-purpose fact checker.
building-genai-apps.labTitle: Python: distinguish malformed structure from an unsupported action
building-genai-apps.setup: Python 3, standard library only. No API key is needed because the model responses are test fixtures.
notes: json.loads parses JSON syntax; the following checks enforce our application’s selected field types.
The evidence lookup checks the pair together, not merely whether the owner exists somewhere in the transcript.
The accepted result remains a draft. This program never sends an email or creates a task.
building-genai-apps.meaning: The first response fails structure, the second fails evidence, and the third reaches the approval stage. One passing check must not stand in for the others. Extend the schema to decisions and every additional field before using this example in a real system.
building-genai-apps.mistake: Repeatedly asking the model to “try again” is not a sufficient fallback. Cap retries, explain missing information, preserve the original evidence, and route unresolved cases to a person.
building-genai-apps.tryIt: Why is a list of valid employee names alone insufficient to validate an action owner?
building-genai-apps.answer: A person can exist without being assigned that action. The evidence must support the relationship between this person and this task, not merely each value separately.
building-genai-apps.output:
REJECT: required fields must be lists
REVIEW: action lacks approved evidence
DRAFT READY: request human approval

genai-deployment.title: Plan for the slow request, the duplicate request, and the failed request
intro: A classroom demo receives one request at a time. A deployed service may receive a burst during a product launch, a client retry after a timeout, or a model-provider outage. Deployment adds the controls that let the application respond predictably when conditions are no longer ideal.

Separate the browser from trusted server work. The browser sends the user’s request; a server authenticates it, applies limits, accesses model credentials, and validates the response. Hosted inference outsources parts of model serving. Self-hosting gives your team more responsibility for hardware, runtime, access control, scaling, and recovery. Neither choice removes application-level checks.
genai-deployment.mechanismTitle: A request ID helps distinguish retrying from doing new work
mechanism: An idempotency key identifies one intended operation so that repeating it does not unintentionally repeat its effect. The server must associate that key with the authenticated user and the request contents; otherwise one user or a different prompt could receive an unrelated cached result.

The toy service below stores completed results in a dictionary and rejects reuse of a key with a different request. It is single-process and sequential. Production requires durable storage, atomic coordination for concurrent duplicates, expiration rules, and provider support where applicable. A local dictionary cannot prevent duplicate provider work after a crash or across several servers.
genai-deployment.labTitle: Python: simulate a retry without repeating a completed generation
genai-deployment.setup: Python 3, standard library only. The model call is a deterministic stand-in, so this tests request handling rather than generation quality.
genai-deployment.code:
cache = {}
model_calls = 0

def generate(user, request_id, prompt):
    global model_calls
    key = (user, request_id)
    if key in cache:
        old_prompt, answer = cache[key]
        if old_prompt != prompt:
            raise ValueError("request ID reused for different input")
        return answer
    model_calls += 1
    answer = f"Draft for: {prompt}"
    cache[key] = (prompt, answer)
    return answer

print(generate("user-1", "req-7", "college invitation"))
print(generate("user-1", "req-7", "college invitation"))
print("Model calls:", model_calls)
try:
    generate("user-1", "req-7", "different task")
except ValueError as error:
    print("Rejected:", error)
print("Average in-flight estimate:", 2 * 3)
notes: The compound key separates users. Storing the original prompt detects accidental or malicious key reuse.
The second identical request returns the saved answer without incrementing the model-call count.
The final calculation uses two requests per second and three seconds average service time; its units simplify to requests.
genai-deployment.meaning: An average of six in-flight requests is a planning estimate, not the amount of capacity to provision. Bursts, slow-tail requests, queues, and retries need measured headroom. Monitor latency, errors, accepted-output cost, and quality together; fast responses are not useful if they are wrong.
genai-deployment.mistake: Do not retry indefinitely or log raw private prompts by default. Use timeouts, bounded backoff for retryable failures, redaction, access-controlled telemetry, and a tested rollback to a known-good version.
genai-deployment.tryIt: What happens if the process crashes after a provider accepts a request but before the result reaches the dictionary?
genai-deployment.answer: The dictionary cannot prove completion. A retry may repeat the billed work. Durable request state and, when supported, provider-side idempotency are needed to handle that uncertainty.
genai-deployment.output:
Draft for: college invitation
Draft for: college invitation
Model calls: 1
Rejected: request ID reused for different input
Average in-flight estimate: 6
